title: Should you build customer feedback analysis in-house with an LLM, or buy a tool?
summary: Should you build customer feedback analysis in-house with an LLM or buy a tool? Buy the analysis layer for consistency, and use LLMs as the interface.
body_markdown:
Most teams asking this question have already run the experiment. Someone exported a survey file and pasted it into ChatGPT or an enterprise large language model (LLM). A tidy list of themes came back in minutes. Now the question is whether to turn that prototype into an internal system or buy a dedicated feedback analytics tool.


The short answer: buy a tool for the analysis, and use LLMs as the interface on top. Building in-house makes sense only when feedback analysis is hard to separate from your core systems. For most customer experience (CX) and insights teams, it's a standalone function. The hard part isn't summarization. Any LLM does that well. The hard part is consistency: the same answer to the same question every month, a theme taxonomy that holds steady, and a score-change waterfall that explains why[net promoter score (NPS)](https://getthematic.com/insights/ultimate-guide-to-net-promoter-score) moved. Thematic is built for that layer. It connects to Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), so teams keep the conversational interface they like.


Below is a decision framework, the evidence from a financial services team that tested the build path, and a checklist to run before you commit either way.


## What "build with an LLM" actually means


Building feedback analysis with an LLM means using a general-purpose model, such as ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini, as the analysis engine instead of a purpose-built platform. It's often confused with building a full analytics platform from scratch. In practice, most "builds" start much smaller.


A typical in-house LLM build includes:


- **A prompt or agent** that reads exported comments and returns themes and summaries.
- **A[data pipeline](https://getthematic.com/insights/infrastructure-requirements-for-ai-text-analytics)** that pulls survey, ticket, or review data into the model.
- **A taxonomy** that someone must define, store, and keep stable across runs.
- **A scoring layer** that links themes to NPS,[customer satisfaction (CSAT)](https://getthematic.com/insights/link-feedback-themes-nps-csat-drivers) , or another metric.
- **A reporting layer** that tracks change over time and explains it to stakeholders.


The first item takes an afternoon. The other four are where the real cost sits. They're what separates a demo from a system your executives will trust.


## Why does ChatGPT give inconsistent answers on customer feedback?


General-purpose LLMs aren't designed to[return the same output twice](https://getthematic.com/insights/why-ai-gives-different-feedback-answers) . Researchers at[Thinking Machines Lab](https://thinkingmachines.ai/blog/defeating-nondeterminism-in-llm-inference/) found that "LLM APIs are still not deterministic in practice," even with temperature set to zero. In one test, they ran the same prompt 1,000 times at temperature zero and got 80 unique completions.


For a one-off summary, that variation is tolerable. For a feedback program, it breaks three things:


1. **Trend tracking.** If the themes change between runs, you can't tell whether customers changed or the model did.
2. **Score attribution.** Explaining a score move requires the same themes, defined the same way, in both periods.
3. **Defensibility.** An answer that changes on the second ask is hard to put in front of a board or a regulator.


The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) Generative AI Profile ([NIST AI 600-1](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/NIST.AI.600-1.pdf) ) names a related risk, confabulation: "The production of confidently stated but erroneous or false content." Plausible themes aren't the same as reliable themes.


## What a financial services team learned by testing an LLM build


A[large financial services provider](https://getthematic.com/case-studies/financial-services) ran a version of this test. The company had a clearly negative NPS from an independent competitive NPS survey, with under a hundred responses a month.


An analyst on the team built an NPS agent on an off-the-shelf enterprise LLM in about an hour, using the same survey export. The agent produced plausible top-level themes. It could not give the same answer twice, build the score-change waterfall, or maintain the taxonomy needed for month-to-month tracking.


The team's conclusion was blunt. Consistency, not summarization, was the thing they needed.


Technology leadership applied a simple rule. Buy externally for a standalone function. Build internally only where the capability is hard to separate from core systems. Feedback analytics was classed as a clear buy.


The team now uses Thematic as the consistent source of truth, with LLMs as the interface on top via MCP. Across the program, NPS improved by more than 20 points, moving from negative to positive. The waterfall showed where the gain came from: the CX and contact team was the largest departmental contributor at roughly 8 points, client communications added roughly 7 points, and fees were a modest drag. The company has since set a further double-digit improvement target.


## How do you decide whether to build or buy?


Use these five questions to decide. If three or more of your answers land in the buy column, buy.


**Question** **Points to build** **Points to buy**


Is feedback analysis hard to separate from core systems? Yes, it is embedded in a proprietary product No, it is a standalone function


Do you need the same answer every month? No, one-off research only Yes, you track trends and targets


Must you explain why a score moved? No Yes, leadership asks for drivers


Who maintains the taxonomy? A dedicated data team with capacity Nobody has time to own it


Will regulators or auditors review the output? No Yes, outputs must be traceable


The[Bank of England and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA)](https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/report/2024/artificial-intelligence-in-uk-financial-services-2024) found in 2024 that 46% of surveyed financial firms have only "partial understanding" of the AI technologies they use. An in-house LLM build widens that gap unless someone owns its behavior over time.


## Where do in-house LLM builds fall short?


In-house builds usually stall at the same points:


- **No stable taxonomy.** Themes are regenerated each run, so last quarter's categories don't match this quarter's.
- **No score linkage.** The model summarizes text but doesn't quantify how much each theme moved NPS.
- **No traceability.** Answers can't be traced back to the specific comments behind them.
- **No owner.** The analyst who built the prototype moves on. The prompt becomes undocumented infrastructure.


A useful test: ask your prototype the same question on two different days and compare the theme lists. If they differ, the build isn't ready to be a source of truth.


## What tools are better suited than ChatGPT for analyzing customer feedback?


If ChatGPT gives you inconsistent answers on customer feedback, the better-suited tool is a dedicated feedback analytics platform that holds the taxonomy steady, with the LLM kept as the interface. Thematic is built for that role.


**Consistent themes.** Thematic builds a two-level theme taxonomy from your feedback and maintains it across periods, so a theme means the same thing month to month. Thematic applies the same themes to older and newer data, so period-over-period comparisons stay like-for-like. Teams refine themes when they choose to. Even without human help, Thematic can get[80 to 90% accurate themes](https://getthematic.com/insights/how-accurate-is-thematic) , depending on the dataset. For context, expert human analysts agree with each other only 40 to 70% of the time, depending on the task.


**Score-change waterfall.** Thematic links scores to the themes driving them through impact and waterfall charts. Teams see which themes pushed NPS up and which pulled it down, period over period.


**Traceability.** In Thematic, every theme and score traces back to the raw customer comments behind it. That's what makes an answer defensible.


**LLMs as the interface.** The[Thematic MCP server](https://getthematic.com/product/mcp-server) connects to Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot. Teams ask questions in plain language, and the answers are pulled from Thematic data rather than generated from scratch. The LLM handles the conversation. Thematic holds the source of truth.


## What should you ask before you build or buy?


Ask these questions before you commit:


1. Does the same question return the same themes on two different days?
2. Can the system show which themes drove a score change, with point values?
3. Does the taxonomy persist month to month without manual rebuilds?
4. Can every insight be traced back to source comments?
5. Who owns the system when the person who built it leaves?
6. Is feedback analysis truly inseparable from your core systems?
7. Can your team still use its preferred LLM as the interface?


## The short answer


For most CX and insights teams, buy the analysis layer and keep LLMs as the interface. Build only where feedback analysis is hard to separate from core systems. A financial services team built an LLM agent in about an hour, found it could not give the same answer twice, and kept Thematic as its consistent source of truth, with LLMs on top via MCP.
